spec.description: What one station reported over a span of time, newest first. A busy airport station such as `KSEA` reports every five minutes, plus an hourly report at 53 minutes past, so a day there is about 300 observations.

station_id.description: Station identifier, such as `KSEA`. `stations.list_stations` returns it as `stationIdentifier`.

start.description: Start of the span, inclusive. The service keeps about a week of observations; a start older than that returns nothing rather than failing.

end.description: End of the span, exclusive: an observation at exactly `end` is not returned.

limit.description: Observations per response. Range [1, 500]; the service caps a response at 500 whether or not this is sent, so 500 is also the default.

response.title: ObservationCollection
response.description: The observations in the span, as a GeoJSON feature collection, newest first.

pagination.title: ObservationPagination
pagination.description: Where the next page is, as a whole URL. The declared walk moves the time window instead and never reads this.

next.description: URL of the next page. Absent on the last one.

notes: The walk is anchored to `end`, measured from the two recordings of the same six hours of KSEA (02:00 to 08:00 on 2026-09-09): `ksea_window` (limit 500) returns all 76 observations, 07:55 back to 02:00, and `ksea_capped` (limit 10) returns 07:55 back to 07:15, the ten newest and exactly the first ten rows of the uncapped response. A capped response keeps the newest rows, so the walk moves `end` and pages newest-first, which is also the order the service answers in.

The cursor is an observation's `timestamp`, which is unique per station: the service builds each observation's `id` from it (`/stations/KSEA/observations/2026-09-09T07:55:00+00:00`). The service treats `start` as inclusive and `end` as exclusive, measured live on 2026-09-28: from 11:00 with `limit=3`, `end=11:55:00Z` answers 11:53, 11:50, 11:45 and `end=11:55:01Z` answers 11:55, 11:53, 11:50. So the request after a full page, which ends at the oldest observation that page held, does not return it again. Inclusivity is not declared (ADR 0013): if the service ever re-served the boundary observation, the walk would drop it by timestamp.

The service also pages this endpoint by cursor, in a `pagination.next` URL. The time window is the walk a caller actually means here -- "what did this station report yesterday" -- and it is the one that can be declared, since the cursor arrives inside a URL rather than on its own.

`limit` declares `default: 500` because that is what the service does, not because it documents it: a six-day span of KSEA observations comes back as exactly 500 rows with `limit` sent and with it omitted. The declared default is the walk's row cap: a response of 500 rows means there is more in the span, and the walk moves `end` back to the oldest timestamp it saw and asks again, instead of taking a capped response as the whole span.
